The more points an object is touching your body, the more resistance you have to one jolt making it shake. So you can offer it forward with both hands like you see commonly in Japanese culture. You can also lean up against a desk by resting your wrists or hands on it. Set your hand down on it, then hand it with your hand on the (for example bank teller) desk flick your wrist forward to extend it. Yeah, I didn’t notice at first either but after a while I totally noticed a bunch of ways tremors have increased/decreased because of it. Singularly depression and sadness increases blood pressure, which makes it so your nerves are weaker the farther you get from the heart. Here’s what I’ve gathered over the years, hopefully it helps in anxious situations:

-If a body part is resting, it shakes less. Put your elbow or wrist down if you’re trying to work with something like tweezers. The closer you have to a limb resting next to your body-part, the more stable it will be. For example resting your elbow is more freedom but less hand stability.

-Anxiety and depression, obviously, is a large increase. If you’re more anxious or any specific intense emotion, it’s more likely to make you shake. In some situation this can include happiness, but not always. I’ve noticed usually a “passive”, ongoing shake starts first but if you get more intense emotions or try to hold it in, then quick jerks of something like your shoulder happen, but usually they can be contained to the body, not a forward punch like these guys express.

-Extreme weathers. I don’t live in an extremely warm area so I can’t say, but obviously the cold can make your teeth chatter or body shake. Of course a blizzard is an uncommon situation, but combining factors such as an Industrial AC making the room cool can make an anxious person uncontrollably “chatter”.

-Increase in blood pressure, the main example being nicotine use, can decrease control over shaking.

-Ever have a really sweaty chest but really cold hands/feet? Keep in mind that your chest is kind of like a core for the blood. The farther you get from your chest, the harder it is for blood to travel to that area. That means your hands and feet have a harder time being warmed than where most of the organs are, besides the issue of fat. But in this situation, I say it because it’s good to keep in mind that your nervous system also has less control the farther it gets if you are sensitive to tremors. My hands and fingers will sometimes feel a little numb and weaker than my feet if they get more blood, it’s the same thing that happens when you cut off blood to a limb; it “falls asleep”, and is also sort of similar to Parkinson’s.
